3: Hold on to what is highest, and you will flourish beyond this world.
5: Those who truly delight in praising God shake off even the deeds done in darkness.
6: Follow the faultless way of the One who mastered the five senses, and you will long prosper.
8: No one swims the sea of wrongdoing alone. Only those who hold the feet of the One who is a sea of goodness can cross it.
9: A head that bows to nothing greater is like a sense that has lost its power — useless.
12: Rain gives us food, and rain itself is our drink. Life runs on it.
13: If the clouds hold back the rain they have taken up, hunger will trouble the whole wide world for a long time.
14: When the wealth-giving rain dries up, even the plough must stop.
15: Rain, when it fails, ruins people. When it falls, it restores their fortune.
16: If not one drop falls from the clouds, not even a blade of green grass will appear.
17: Even the wealth of the wide sea would shrink if the cloud that draws up its water never gave it back as rain.
18: If the sky dries up, neither the daily offerings nor the yearly festivals can happen on earth.
19: Without rain, prayer and charity cannot live in this wide world.
21: The highest aim of all books is to praise those who give up every desire while living rightly where they are.
22: Trying to measure the greatness of those free of all desire is like counting the dead — there is no end to it.
23: The greatness of those who understand both worlds and let them go shines brightest on earth.
24: Rule your five senses with the hook of wisdom, and you plant yourself a place in heaven.
25: Even Indra, king of heaven, stands as proof of the power of those who master their senses.
26: Great people do what is hard to do. Small minds cannot.
27: The world lies open to the one who truly understands what taste, sight, touch, hearing, and smell bring.
28: The quiet, weighty words of the truly great show their greatness to the world.
29: Even a flash of anger from those who have climbed the mountain of goodness is something the world cannot withstand.
30: The good are truly called holy because they are wrapped in kindness toward every living thing.
31: Virtue gives both heaven and wealth. What greater happiness could anyone hold?
32: Nothing brings more good than practicing virtue. Nothing brings more evil than forgetting it.
34: Do good with a clean heart. Without that, goodness is only a show.
35: That is true virtue which is free of four things: malice, desire, anger, and harsh speech.
36: Do not put virtue off to another day. Take it up today, and it will be your friend at the hour of death.
37: The reward of virtue needs no book to explain it — just look at the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it.
38: Do some good every single day, and you block the door to being born again.
39: Only the joy that comes from a good home life is real joy. Everything else brings no praise.
40: Virtue is what you should do. Vice is what you should avoid. It is that simple.
41: A true householder stands as a firm support for all good people around him.
42: He truly flourishes in family life who helps the forsaken, the poor, and even the dead with a proper farewell.
43: A householder's first duty is the five-fold care: for ancestors, gods, guests, relatives, and himself.
44: His family line will never fail — the one who fears wrongdoing while earning, and shares his food with others.
45: When home life holds love and virtue, doing right becomes its own reward.
46: If you live a good life at home, what more could you gain by walking away from it?
47: Of all who labor for a better life, the greatest is the one who lives well as a householder.
48: The householder who stays true to virtue and helps others on their way endures more than the ascetic at his penance.
49: Family life is true virtue. The ascetic path is good too, if it draws no blame.
50: Whoever lives the married life as it should be lived will stand among the gods in heaven.
51: A wife who manages the home well and spends within her husband's means is his true support.
52: Without goodness in the home, all other greatness counts for nothing.
53: If his wife is virtuous, what does he lack? If she is not, what does he have?
54: Is there anything better than a wife who is steadfastly faithful?
55: A wife devoted to her husband is held to have such grace that even rain would follow her word.
56: A true wife guards herself with care, looks after her husband, and keeps a clean name.
57: No wall or prison guard protects like one's own faithfulness.
58: Women who honor their households, tradition says, will be held great in the world of the gods.
59: A man whose wife cares nothing for a good name cannot hold his head high before those who mock him.
60: A wife's excellence is her husband's good; good children are the jewels of that goodness.
61: Of all the things worth gaining, none is greater than children of good sense.
62: No evil of any birth will touch those whose children are free from vice.
63: People call their sons their wealth, because children carry on their good deeds for them.
64: Rice touched by a child's little hand tastes sweeter to a parent than nectar.
65: A child's touch delights the body; a child's words delight the ear.
66: "The flute is sweet, the lute is sweet" — say those who have never heard their own child's babble.
67: The finest thing a father can do for his son is make the learned receive him with honor.
68: Nothing pleases good people on this earth more than seeing their children learned.
69: A mother delights more in hearing her son called wise than she did on the day he was born.
70: A son's duty to his father: live so that people ask, "What great penance gave him such a son?"
71: No lock can hold in love. The tears of the loving reveal what is inside.
72: Those without love keep everything for themselves. Those with love would give even their bones away.
73: They say our soul and body are joined as the fruit of love and virtue in a former life.
74: Love grows into attachment, and attachment into friendship beyond measure.
75: A life filled with love bears fruits of peace like these.
76: The simple say love only helps virtue. In truth, it also pulls people out of wrongdoing.
77: Virtue scorches a soul without love, just as the sun scorches the softest, boneless creatures.
78: A home without love is like a dead tree standing in a dry desert.
79: Without love — the inner sense — what use are any of the outer senses?
80: Only a body filled with love holds a living soul. Without it, it is just bone wrapped in skin.
81: The whole point of family life and saving wealth is to have the means to welcome guests.
82: However fine your own meal, it is wrong to wish your guests away from the door.
83: The home that feeds its guests every day will never be ruined by poverty.
84: The goddess of fortune gladly lives in the house that welcomes good guests with a smile.
85: He who feeds his guests first and eats what remains need never plough a field — plenty finds him.
86: Whoever feeds those who come and watches for more to come will be an honored guest in heaven.
87: The goodness of hospitality cannot be measured. The guest himself is its only measure.
88: Those who never practiced hospitality will grieve at last: "We toiled and stored up wealth, and now we have no one."
89: To hoard wealth while turning guests away is true poverty. It is the fool's way.
90: A guest wilts before a cold face, as the anicham flower wilts at a single sniff.
91: Sweet words are words of love, free of deceit, spoken by the good.
92: A kind word and a smiling face are worth more than a generous gift.
93: Speech that flows warmly from the heart, with a bright face — that is true virtue.
94: Sweet speech that delights everyone keeps sorrowful poverty away.
95: Humility and sweet speech are a person's true ornaments. Everything else is not.
96: Speak usefully and sweetly, and your faults fade while your goodness grows.
97: Words that help and please at the same time bring goodness in this world and the next.
98: Sweet words that hurt no one bring joy both here and hereafter.
99: If sweet words bring such joy, why would anyone choose harsh ones?
100: Choosing harsh words when sweet ones are ready is like eating unripe fruit when ripe fruit is at hand.
101: A kindness given when nothing was owed outweighs heaven and earth.
102: A small favor given at the right time is worth more than the world.
103: A kindness given without counting the return is bigger than the sea.
104: Though the help be small as a millet seed, the grateful hold it as large as a palm fruit.
105: A favor is not measured by its size, but by how the one who received it honors it.
106: Never drop a friend who stood by you in hard times. Never forget the kindness of the blameless.
107: The wise remember, through all their births, those who wiped away their sorrow.
109: Even a great injury melts away in the face of one kindness remembered.
110: Whoever betrays every virtue may still find escape. The one who betrays a kindness will find none.
111: Treating enemies, strangers, and friends with the same even hand is a virtue above the rest.
112: The wealth of the fair-minded never perishes — it blesses their children too.
113: Drop, on the spot, any gain that comes unfairly, however profitable it looks.
114: A person's worth shows in whether their children turn out good.
115: Loss and gain never come without reason. The wise stay even-minded through both.
116: Whoever sets fairness aside to do wrong should tell themselves plainly: "I am heading for ruin."
117: The great never see the fair-minded person's modest means as poverty.
118: To lean to neither side, steady as a balanced scale — that is the wise person's mark.
119: Honest words count only when the mind behind them is honest too.
120: The truest business is to guard and treat another's goods exactly as you would your own.
121: Self-control raises a person to the gods. Its lack drags one into the darkest dark.
122: Guard self-control like a treasure. Nothing brings a person more good.
123: Self-control itself is knowledge. Whoever masters themselves wins honor among the wise.
124: Greater than a mountain grows the one who stays in family life yet keeps full command of themselves.
125: Humility befits everyone. In the rich, it is a wealth greater than riches.
126: Hold in your five senses like the tortoise for even one lifetime, and that guard will protect all your births.
127: If you guard nothing else, guard your tongue. Every slip of it brings misery.
128: One evil word can turn all your good into evil.
129: A wound burnt by fire may heal. A wound burnt by the tongue never heals.
130: Virtue will find the person who, with learning and self-control, keeps anger away.
